questions.prompt: What is the most constructive next step?
questions.context: Five support a city-funded transportation pilot; two object over costs. The task asks for unanimity.

options.text: Declare that five votes are enough.
options.feedback: Not quite. A majority does not resolve objections when seeking unanimity.

options.text: Ask the concerned participants what changes would make the proposal acceptable.
options.feedback: Correct. Understanding concerns opens a path to negotiation.

options.text: Ignore objections and move to the summary.
options.feedback: Not quite. Ignoring concerns prevents meaningful consensus.

questions.context: The two participants could support the pilot if initial costs are limited.

options.text: Propose a limited pilot with a spending cap and evaluation before expansion.
options.feedback: Correct. This addresses the concern while retaining the proposal.

options.text: Your concerns are holding everyone back.
options.feedback: Not quite. Criticism makes negotiation harder.
Not quite. A workable compromise deserves consideration first.

questions.context: A possible compromise has emerged, but only two minutes remain.

options.text: Begin an extended debate on unrelated alternatives.
options.feedback: Not quite. This distracts from a timely decision.

options.text: State the revised recommendation and ask whether substantial concerns remain.
options.feedback: Correct. A focused check tests whether the compromise is supported.
Not quite. Silence alone does not establish support.
